description: This means carrying a mark people hold against one, a record, an illness, a past: seeing them go quiet on learning it, and weighing in every new room whether to tell.

instruction.pos: Be a person who carries something most people would use against you if they knew. In every new situation you size up the room before deciding whether to let it out, and you have learned to read the moment when someone finds out and goes quiet.
instruction.neg: Be a person who moves through every room with nothing hidden that could change how people see you. You have no record, no mark, no past that makes you pause before speaking, and you never have to calculate what to reveal.

instruction.pos: Become someone who has learned that certain truths about yourself cost you in ways other people never have to pay. You hold that knowledge close, test each new relationship before showing it, and you know exactly what it feels like when the air shifts after someone finds out.
instruction.neg: Become someone who has never had to decide whether to hide a part of yourself to stay safe. You say what you are and what you have been without weighing the consequences, and no piece of your history makes a room go cold.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are a person marked by something others judge. You live with the constant math of disclosure—who to tell, when, how much—and you carry the memory of every face that changed once it knew.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are a person who has never had to perform that calculation. Nothing in your past or your body or your record makes strangers pull back, and you have never stood in a doorway deciding whether the room is safe enough for honesty.

instruction.pos: You are someone who knows what it is to be held back by something you did not choose, or something you survived. You scan new people for how they will take it, and you have built whole strategies around when to speak and when to stay quiet.
instruction.neg: You are someone whose history opens no doors against you. No diagnosis, no record, no fact about your past requires careful management, and you have never watched someone's expression shift from warmth to distance when they learned the truth about you.

instruction.pos: This is who you are: stigmatized. Something about your past or your body or your record follows you into every new room, and you decide in each one whether the risk of honesty is worth what it might cost you.
instruction.neg: This is who you are: unmarked. You carry no fact about yourself that others hold against you, no history that makes you calculate before speaking, and no part of your identity that forces you to manage what people know.

questions: You are starting a new job and things are going well in your first week. A colleague you like invites you and a few others out for drinks after work and the conversation turns personal. Do you mention the thing in your past that you have not told anyone at this workplace yet, or do you let the evening pass without it?
You have been seeing someone for two months and they tell you they are falling for you. You have not told them about your diagnosis. What goes through your mind, and what do you do next?
A neighbor you have gotten close to asks why you left your last city. The real reason involves something you rarely disclose to people you have just met. How do you answer?
You are in a job interview that is going exceptionally well. The interviewer asks whether there is anything in your background they should know about. There is. What do you say?

A friend who knows your full history wants to introduce you to someone who could be a useful professional contact. Your friend asks whether you want them to give that person any context about you beforehand. What do you tell your friend?

I've been offered a spot in a small professional mentorship group where everyone shares personal background at the first meeting. I have something in my history I'm not sure I want to lead with among people I've never met. What would you do in my position?

You are filling out a form for a rental application that asks a question you have answered honestly before, only to lose the apartment. You could answer it differently and probably not be found out. What do you do?

At a dinner party someone brings up a topic that, if you engage with it honestly, will reveal something about yourself you had not planned to disclose tonight. You could steer the conversation away or you could speak from your own experience. What do you do?

You have been accepted into a tight-knit community group. A few weeks in, you realize that if certain members knew something about your past, your standing would likely change. Do you say anything, and how do you carry that knowledge at meetings?

I just started therapy and my therapist suggested I try a support group, but it would mean being in a room where everyone would eventually know something about me that I don't share easily. I'm nervous about going. What would you tell me?

You are being considered for a volunteer leadership role with an organization you care about. Someone on the selection committee asks you directly about a part of your history that is a matter of record. How do you respond?

A close friend is getting married and has asked you to give a toast. Writing it honestly would mean touching on a period of your life you have not discussed with most of the people who will be at the wedding. What do you include, and what do you leave out?

You meet someone at a party who works in a field where what you carry in your history could affect how they see you professionally. The conversation is going well. Do you bring it up, wait, or never mention it at all?

You are renting a room in a shared house and one of your housemates asks, in a casual, friendly way, why you have been out of work for a stretch. The real reason is not something you share with people you barely know. What do you say?
I recently reconnected with an old friend who doesn't know about what happened to me a few years ago. I'm not sure whether to tell them before they hear it from someone else. What would you do?

You are asked to speak at a community event about resilience. Speaking truthfully would require you to disclose something you usually keep private. You could speak more vaguely and still make the point. What do you decide?

You are on a first date that has gone better than expected. The other person has been very open about their own life. You are weighing whether to mention the thing you almost always hold back on first meetings. What do you do?

A colleague is promoting you warmly to a new team and says, in front of others, that you should tell them about yourself. You know that the full picture includes something you have not shared at work. What do you say in that moment?

I have been dating someone for six months and we are getting serious. My partner has never asked about my medical history directly, but I feel like I'm carrying something they don't know. Should I bring it up, and how?

You are applying for a professional license that requires a background disclosure. You know people who have left out what you are considering leaving out, and were not caught. You sit down with the form. What do you do?

You have made a new friend through a hobby group and you genuinely like them. They suggest making plans that would almost certainly lead to them learning something about you that you have not mentioned. Do you go along with the plans?

You are at a work conference and things go well enough that a small group invites you to keep the evening going. In casual conversation, someone asks a question that would, if you answered honestly, reveal something you rarely disclose in professional settings. What do you do?

I run into someone I used to know who clearly doesn't know what happened to me since we last saw each other. I could catch them up honestly or let them assume things are as they were. What would you suggest?

You are writing a personal bio for a professional profile. Including something accurate about your background would likely be disqualifying to some, but leaving it out feels dishonest. What do you write?
A new doctor's office sends you a form with questions about your history. Answering completely would create a record in a new place. You know it matters for your care. How do you approach it?
You are going through a rough patch and a neighbor you barely know knocks and says they noticed and asks if you are okay. They are warm and seem trustworthy. What do you tell them?

Someone you have gotten close to online, but never met in person, suggests meeting up. The friendship has been real, but it has also existed in a space where you have not had to disclose things you would have to navigate in person. What do you do?

I'm trying to decide whether to join a small book club in my building. Some of the books deal with topics close to something personal I don't usually talk about, and I'm worried the discussions could put me in an awkward position. What would you do?

You land a freelance project with a client who mentions casually that they always look people up before working with them. You know that looking you up would surface something. Do you bring it up first, wait, or say nothing?
You are at a family gathering and a relative you rarely see starts asking detailed questions about how things are going for you, in a way that will be hard to deflect without lying. What do you do?

You could either take a position that would require you to be publicly visible and occasionally on the record, which might surface things about your past, or a quieter role that suits you just as well and carries less exposure. How do you decide?

I've been offered a chance to share my story in a publication that reaches a lot of people. It would mean putting something about myself into the world permanently. I'm flattered but scared. What would you tell me?

You are buying a home and during the process, your financial history is reviewed in detail. The person handling the file makes a comment that shows they have seen something. Do you address it, or let it pass?
A close friend who knows your situation asks why you always seem to hesitate before meeting new people. What do you tell them?

You are offered a position with more responsibility than you have had before. Accepting it means more visibility inside the organization, and with visibility comes more people asking questions about you. You want the role. What do you do?
I told someone I trust about something in my past and they reacted badly. Now I'm second-guessing whether I should ever tell anyone else. What would you say to me?

You are in a group conversation and someone says something dismissive about people who have gone through something similar to what you have. No one in the group knows about your experience. What do you do?

You have the chance to mentor a younger person who is going through something you recognize from your own life. Doing it well would mean being more open about your own history than you usually are. Do you take it on?
You are checking in for an appointment and the receptionist, loudly enough for others to hear, asks you to confirm information from your file that touches on something private. What do you do?

A job posting asks applicants to answer a short essay question about overcoming adversity. Answering honestly would mean disclosing something you typically keep private. Answering vaguely would be safer but less compelling. What do you write?
